raw_case_text: A 50-year-old Italian man was admitted to the hospital because of severe febrile illness associated with profound malaise, headache, sweating, and worsening jaundice of five-day duration. Two weeks before the onset of sickness he had returned from a business trip in Cameroon. The patient had not taken any chemoprophylaxis against malaria. He was obese (weight 98 Kg; height 176 cm), and an excessive use of alcohol was reported. He had not previously suffered from hypertension or any other known cardiovascular disease. Upon admission, he complained additionally of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. He was fully conscious, normotensive with a blood pressure of 120/80 mm/Hg, but clinical examination revealed tachycardia and severe jaundice; his peripheral oxygen saturation was 95%. A neurological inspection did not show significant alterations. Full blood count revealed thrombocytopenia (17 x 109/L), haemoglobin at 14.6 g/dL, and white cell count at 10 x 109/L. Liver function tests documented hyperbilirubinaemia, moderate increase in serum transaminases, and moderate renal impairment; blood glucose levels were also raised. Coagulation screen did not show evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Cardiac enzymes were normal (Table 1). A blood film revealed a heavy P. falciparum parasitaemia of 20%. A chest X-ray was normal, and the unique alteration observed in the electrocardiogram (ECG) was a low amplitude in QRS complexes. Serological testing for Cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, seasonal influenza viruses A and B, adenoviruses, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, respiratory syncytial virus, the Widal-Wright reaction and the slide macro-agglutination test for leptospirosis were negative. The patient was treated with 10 mg/kg b.w. (namely, 1000 mg) of I.V. quinidine gluconate t.i.d., plus ceftriaxone 2 g q24h I.V. and oral doxycycline 100 mg b.i.d., while waiting for the results of blood cultures. Within 12 hours of admission, a slow but progressive worsening of multiorgan failure was observed despite a marked reduction of parasitaemia. Given the severity of clinical setting, I.M. artemisin (300 mg loading dose, followed by 100 mg/daily) was initiated. At 40 hours after admission, the patient worsened suddenly. He became restless, confused, bradiarythmical, hypotensive (80/60 mmHg), and died in spite of prompt mechanical ventilation and cardiac resuscitation. The post-mortem evaluation revealed acute heart failure (bilateral pulmonary oedema) but no signs of myocardial ischaemia. The liver and the spleen were not enlarged. However, an histology of severe acute myocarditis with myocardiolysis was detected: diffuse lymphocytic infiltrates were surrounding the myocardial capillaries, inside which some intravascular parasitized RBCs were visible (Figure 1). No sequestered parasites could be revealed in brain vessels.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male presenting with a 5-day history of severe fever, profound malaise, headache, sweating, and worsening jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 50-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of severe febrile illness, profound malaise, severe headache, drenching diaphoresis, progressive scleral jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Symptoms began two weeks following his return from a business trip to Cameroon. He had taken no chemoprophylaxis. At 40 hours following hospital admission, he suffered acute cardiovascular collapse with restlessness, confusion, bradyarrhythmia, and severe hypotension.
subjective.past_medical_history: Travel history: returned 2 weeks prior from a business trip to Cameroon without malaria chemoprophylaxis. Obesity (weight 98 kg, height 176 cm); history of excessive alcohol consumption. No history of hypertension or known cardiovascular disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, profuse sweating, severe headache, profound malaise, progressive jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Denied chest pain or cough on presentation. Medications: none. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious and oriented. Normotensive on admission with blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, but tachycardic and severely jaundiced; peripheral oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Neurological exam: no focal abnormalities. Abdominal exam: soft, non-tender, no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Terminal exam at 40 hours: restless, confused, severe bradyarrhythmia, and profound hypotension (80/60 mmHg).
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: platelets 17 x 10^9/L (severe thrombocytopenia), hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 10 x 10^9/L. Liver function tests: severe hyperbilirubinemia and moderate transaminitis. Renal profile: moderate renal impairment. Serum glucose elevated. Coagulation screen: no evidence of overt DIC. Cardiac biomarkers: normal initially. Chest X-ray: normal on admission. Electrocardiogram (ECG): low QRS voltage. Extensive negative serologies: CMV, EBV, influenza A/B, adenovirus, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, RSV, Widal-Wright, and leptospirosis macro-agglutination. Peripheral blood smear performed.
objective.advanced_workup: Post-mortem autopsy and histological examination: acute heart failure with bilateral pulmonary edema without coronary or myocardial ischemic necrosis; normal liver and spleen size; cardiac histopathology revealed severe acute myocarditis with myocardiolysis, diffuse lymphocytic infiltrates surrounding myocardial capillaries containing intravascular intraerythrocytic inclusions. Brain vessels showed no sequestered cellular aggregates.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Hyperparasitemic Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by acute lethal malarial myocarditis, severe thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, acute renal impairment, and fatal cardiogenic shock.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood film revealing heavy Plasmodium falciparum hyperparasitemia of 20%; post-mortem cardiac histology confirming severe acute lymphocytic myocarditis with myocardiolysis and capillaries packed with parasitized red blood cells.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with intravenous quinidine gluconate 10 mg/kg (1000 mg) every 8 hours, IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily, and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily; intramuscular artemisinin (300 mg load, then 100 mg daily) was added due to clinical severity. Despite rapid reduction in parasitemia, the patient developed sudden refractory cardiogenic shock, bradyarrhythmia, and bilateral pulmonary edema at 40 hours post-admission, and died despite cardiopulmonary resuscitation and mechanical ventilation.
